title: At the café
description: Order a drink, read the room, and ask for the bill.

explanation.summary: Spanish nouns have a gender, and the article shows it. Usually el is masculine and la is feminine. You have to learn the gender with the word, because there is no way to work it out from the word itself.

sections.heading: The two articles
sections.body: El is masculine and la is feminine, and they are the only articles you need for a countable noun in the singular. In the plural they become los and las. A few nouns change their vowel in the plural: el café becomes los cafés, el sofá becomes los sofás.

sections.heading: The endings that usually tell you
sections.body: Most nouns ending in -o are masculine and most ending in -a are feminine: el trabajo, la casa. Nouns ending in -e are usually feminine: la leche, el café is the exception. Nouns ending in a consonant are usually masculine: el reloj, el vaso. But there are exceptions, and they are common enough that you should learn the gender with the noun.

sections.heading: When there is no article
sections.body: The article goes missing in three common cases. After a word for wanting or needing you use un or una: quiero un café. After a number you use de: dos cafés. And with a description the article stays: el café caliente. After a word for a profession the article is left out too, and you will meet that in A1/3.

exercises.prompt: Pair each word with its translation.
exercises.note: Every noun is either masculine or feminine, and the article says which.
Masculine: el café. The plural is los cafés.
